headline: Supermarket Chain Plants 2,150 Heritage Apple Trees to Revive Lost Varieties
meta_description: The Spar Group is testing heirloom apple varieties like the Ilzer Rose in commercial orchards, hoping to bring forgotten flavors back to European supermarkets.
summary_short: A major European supermarket chain is scaling up production of heritage apple varieties forgotten by industrial agriculture, starting with trial runs in Vienna.
body:
One of Europe's largest supermarket chains is attempting something most would consider commercially risky: bringing heritage apples back to market at scale. The Spar Group, working with Austrian produce trader Frutura, has planted 2,150 trees of heirloom varieties in an experimental orchard in Styria, with the first fruits harvested this month for trial runs at Vienna markets. The two varieties being tested—the Ilzer Rose, originating in 1840, and the Falchs Gulderling, identified in the 1870s—represent a deliberate reversal of industrial agriculture's narrowing of choice.

Today's supermarkets typically stock only 3 to 5 apple varieties despite 7,500 existing globally, a legacy of breeding programs designed for high yields, pest resistance, and consistent appearance rather than taste or character. Modern cultivars are optimized for industrial farming in ways that heritage varieties may never be. Yet Spar's deputy chair Markus Kaser sees something shifting in consumer behavior. "Many consumers today are once again taking a greater interest in where food comes from, the varieties involved and how it tastes," he told the Guardian. If the Styrian experiment succeeds, the company plans to expand these "special varieties throughout the region."

What makes this venture more than nostalgic is the recognition that heritage apples carry something besides flavor—they embody agricultural knowledge accumulated over centuries. That lost apple varieties once numbered around 17,000 in North America alone during the 18th and 19th centuries suggests how much diversity industrial farming has erased. Frutura's co-managing director described tasting the Ilzer Rose and Gulderling as evoking childhood memories, a quality that reflects both flavor and history. Whether consumers will embrace apples grown with more difficulty for less predictable yields remains uncertain, but Spar's willingness to test the market suggests confidence that some shoppers hunger for more than convenience.
quick_facts: Spar Group testing 2,150 heritage apple trees in Styria, Austria
First varieties: Ilzer Rose (1840) and Falchs Gulderling (1870s)
Modern supermarkets stock 3-5 varieties despite 7,500 existing apples
Fruits harvested and sent for trial runs in Vienna markets
